blocks.text: 4. Why Some Models Need Split Inference

blocks.alt: Why Some Models Need Split Inference
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446562920-189624623.png

This connects back to recapping scaling to multiple server instances, already covered in this topic. Genuinely some very large models genuinely cannot fit entirely on one single GPU, even just for inference.

This is already covered generally as model parallelism in Multi-GPU Training, the exact same limitation now applies at serving time too, a genuinely direct carryover explored throughout the rest of this topic.
5. Pipeline Parallelism In Inference
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446562921-25841199.png

This connects back to why some models need split inference, already covered in this topic. One genuinely approach assigns different genuinely layers of the model to different genuinely devices in sequence.
Genuinely each request flows through those devices one after another, like stations along a pipeline, the exact first strategy explored throughout the rest of this topic.
6. Tensor Parallelism In Inference
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446562922-279125386.png
This connects back to pipeline parallelism in inference, already covered in this topic. An alternative genuinely splits individual weight matrices themselves across multiple devices instead.
Genuinely every device genuinely computes part of the exact same layer's own output, in parallel, for every single request, the exact second strategy explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 7. Latency Impact Of Splitting Inference
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446562922-589354973.png

This connects back to tensor parallelism in inference, already covered in this topic. Splitting a genuinely single model across devices genuinely requires communication between those devices for every request.

This is already covered generally as latency budgets in Real-Time Inference, this genuinely communication cost matters especially strongly here, a genuinely real, practical tradeoff explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 8. When To Split Versus Replicate
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446562923-384208525.png
This connects back to the latency impact of splitting inference, already covered in this topic. A genuinely model that fits on one device is genuinely better simply replicated many times instead.

Splitting a genuinely single model across devices genuinely only makes sense when it genuinely does not fit otherwise, a genuinely clear, practical decision rule explored throughout the rest of this topic.
9. Recognizing When Distributed Inference Is Genuinely Necessary

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Distributed Inference Is Genuinely Necessary

This connects back to why some models need split inference, already covered in this topic. Distributed inference, already covered in this topic, genuinely serves models too large for a single device.

This connects back to recapping scaling to multiple server instances, already covered generally in Serving. Simple replication, already covered generally in Serving, remains genuinely simpler and sufficient for smaller models.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates simulating pipeline parallelism, already covered in this topic, passing a request through sequential simulated devices.

code.content:
def device_layer(input_value, weight, device_id):
    # already covered as different layers assigned to different devices in this topic
    output = input_value * weight
    print(f"Device {device_id} (already covered as pipeline parallelism in this topic): input={input_value:.3f}, output={output:.3f}")
    return output

# already covered as splitting the model's own layers across devices in this topic
model_layers = [
    {"weight": 1.2, "device_id": 0},
    {"weight": 0.8, "device_id": 1},
    {"weight": 1.5, "device_id": 2},
]

def run_pipeline_inference(request_input, model_layers):
    current_value = request_input
    for layer in model_layers:
        current_value = device_layer(current_value, layer["weight"], layer["device_id"])
    return current_value

print("Running one request through the split model's own pipeline (already covered in this topic):\n")
final_output = run_pipeline_inference(request_input=1.0, model_layers=model_layers)
print(f"\nFinal output after passing through every device: {final_output:.3f}")

blocks.text: 11. MLOps for Deep Learning: Module Complete

items: Distributed inference spreads a single model's own inference workload across multiple devices.
It goes beyond simple replication, already covered in Serving, by splitting one model itself.
Some very large models cannot fit entirely on one GPU, even just for inference.
Pipeline parallelism assigns different layers to different devices, processed in sequence.
Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices, with devices computing parts in parallel.
Splitting a model across devices requires per-request communication, a real latency cost.
A model that fits on one device is better replicated; splitting only makes sense when it does not fit.
Distributed inference suits models too large for one device; replication suits smaller models.
